title: The King Who Built a Mountain in Stone
sources: Brihadisvara Temple (Wikipedia / Wikiwand): built by Rajaraja I between 1003 and 1010 CE and named Rajarajesvaram; granite temple with a 13-tier vimana; inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 1987 (Great Living Chola Temples, extended 2004).
Rajaraja I (Wikipedia / Wikiwand): reigned c. 985 to 1014 CE; conquests in the Pandya and Chera countries and northern Sri Lanka; land survey of 1000 CE; Thanjavur as the Chola capital.

Wisdomlib, 'Middle Chola Temples' (Rajarajesvara temple, Tanjavur): earliest reference in Rajaraja's 19th regnal year; the copper pot for the finial (stupi-kudam) was handed over to the temple authorities on the 275th day of his 25th year, c. 1010 CE; gifts by the king, his elder sister and his queens were ordered recorded on the srivimana.

South Indian Inscriptions vol. II, Tanjavur temple inscriptions nos. 1-2 (whatisindia.com): gifts of gold vessels, ornaments and images in the 25th-29th years; part of the gold from treasure taken after defeating the Chera and Pandya kings; gifts by the king's elder sister Kundavai.

South Indian Inscriptions vol. II, Tanjavur temple inscription no. 66 (whatisindia.com), 29th year of Rajaraja: 400 temple women, each assigned a house on a temple street and a share of land produce, and 108 male servants (dancing-masters, singers, drummers, accountants, lamp-lighters, barbers and others) with shares.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Great Living Chola Temples' (ref. 250): the Brihadisvara complex remains an active place of worship.

Not stated as fact in the film: the temple height (sources disagree, about 60-66 m), the earth-ramp theory of construction, and any likeness of the king. The 80-ton capstone is narrated as 'traditionally said'. All people and the portrait are illustrations.
